newsitem.title: UK: Depreciation - a way out of trouble for Europe.
newsitem.headline: Depreciation - a way out of trouble for Europe.

text.p: The dollar's impressive rally is as much a symptom of weakness of European currencies as its own intrinsic strength amid a growing perception in the market that currency depreciation is the only way out for Europe.

Depreciation is anathema to most administrations who see currency strength as a sign of economic virility, but in the run up to EMU it may become a necessity in order to get growth going, analysts said.

"There is a growing perception that with European growth weak, interest rates low and fiscal policy being tightened, currency depreciation in Europe is really the only way out," said Robert Hayward, economic adviser at BankAmerica.
"That idea has crystallised in the market's mind overnight."

Bundesbank chief economist Otmar Issing told a bankers' forum on Monday that one of the possible effects of the approach of the single currency was a shift out of the mark into dollar-denominated investments.

This on top of recent calls from European officials for a higher dollar sparked an eight centime rally in dollar/French franc to a 5.3230 peak, a three pfennig rally in dollar/mark to 1.5735 and a 27 lire rise in dollar/lira to a high of 1,544.00.
Sterling's overall devaluation in 1992 after it crashed out of the European exchange rate mechanism (ERM) sparked a meaty economic recovery via improved export competitiveness.

But core Europe is only interested in seeing currencies come down against those outside of Europe. The last thing they want is to spark intra-European wrangles over competitiveness by talking their currencies down against each other.
"In order to get any sort of economic growth they have to try and devalue the core European currencies against the non-European bloc," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.
This opens up two possibilities, devaluation against the yen and or devaluation against the dollar.
Coming down against the yen is a problem given that figures on Tuesday showed Japan is in as poor economic shape as Europe and has only narrowly avoided a technical recession.
That leaves the dollar and as long as U.S. growth looks good the administration is happy with a firmer dollar, but if growth slows it could be a different story.
American firms have already accused Japan of manipulating currency markets for its own ends and warned that it will result in slower U.S. growth.
"The Japanese, and to some extent the Europeans...seem to be looking to export away their problems," National Association of Manufacturers President Jerry Jasinowski said last month.
As the dollar continues to rise cries of anguish from U.S. industry can only get louder.
"That is were the big hole opens up in European strategy, if we see a slowdown in the U.S. there will be problems," CIBC's Coleman said. "This is not a risk free strategy.
